scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for someone to avoid friendships with women because of these territorial feelings they have. Let me start by understanding the situation better. There's this guy, let's call him John, who works in an office. He sits at the same table as a girl, let's say her name is Sarah. They talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently, Sarah has started asking John to go out for drinks on Friday after work, as friends, not as a date. At first, John made excuses for a couple of weeks, but then Sarah asked him if he disliked her. John decided to be honest and told her that he doesn't do friendships with women. He explained that if he spends prolonged time with a woman, he starts feeling territorial. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them, his intestines start roiling, and he feels an extreme sense of agitation. He mentioned that he never acts on it and puts on a happy face and perseveres, but he hates these feelings and prefers to avoid them, hence why he doesn't do friendships with women. Sarah then suggested that John should see a psychologist, but he doesn't want to, even though he knows he's flawed. He believes his flaws make up part of who he is, and he doesn't want to change. Since then, for the past couple of weeks, their talking has just been work-related. John thought it would be best to be honest, but now he's thinking maybe he should have made up some excuse instead. He's asking if this is AITA (Ask if it's AITA, which I think means "Am I the Asshole?"). John also added that he gets the same feelings at work but doesn't think about work at home, so he has no choice but to tolerate them. However, he doesn't want to put himself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. He knows it's not correct, but he can't help feeling this way. He mentioned that he never acts on these feelings. He also told this story to a guy he knows, and that guy said John must have been controlling with his previous girlfriends. John is clarifying that this couldn't be further from the truth. If the lady is already his, he doesn't mind her talking to or being around other guys because he knows she's his, and it makes him happy thinking that other men might want what he has and can't have it. Alright, so breaking this down, John is avoiding friendships with women because of these territorial feelings that cause him discomfort. He's honest with Sarah about this, which led to some tension, and now their interactions are limited to work-related topics. He's questioning whether he should have been more dishonest and just made up excuses instead of being truthful. I need to assess whether John's approach is right or wrong. To do that, I should consider several factors: the impact on his relationships, the authenticity of his approach, the potential for personal growth, and the broader implications of his behavior. First, being honest with Sarah seems like a positive trait because it builds trust. However, his honesty led to a negative outcome where their relationship became strained. This raises the question of whether honesty is always the best policy, especially when it can hurt someone's feelings. Second, avoiding friendships with women because of territorial feelings might be limiting his social life and potentially his personal growth. By avoiding these situations, he's preventing himself from challenging these feelings and possibly overcoming them. Third, his territorial feelings could stem from deeper insecurities or fears. Avoiding the situation doesn't address the root cause, which might be beneficial to explore, perhaps with a psychologist, as Sarah suggested. Fourth, his clarification that he's not controlling in his relationships is important. It shows that his behavior isn't about controlling others but more about his internal feelings of discomfort. Fifth, the fact that he doesn't act on these feelings is crucial. He's not letting his emotions dictate his actions, which is a responsible approach. Lastly, his decision to be honest versus making up excuses is a moral dilemma. On one hand, honesty is valued, but on the other hand, it can sometimes lead to unnecessary conflict or hurt feelings. Considering all these points, I think John's approach has both pros and cons. While honesty is commendable, it's important to consider the impact on others and whether there's a more constructive way to handle these feelings. Perhaps finding a balance between being honest and maintaining positive relationships could be a better approach.
